lessons.title: Are we there yet?
lessons.goal: Buckle up, ask how much longer, and ask for music on a road trip.

dialogue.es: ¡Vamos a Tucson! Abróchate el cinturón, Mateo.
dialogue.en: Let's go to Tucson! Buckle your seat belt, Mateo.
Mom, put some music on, please.
A red car! Mom, are we there yet?

tip.title: Ya and todavía
tip.text: In ¿Ya llegamos?, ya means already or yet, so it asks are we there yet? Todavía no means not yet. Abróchate ends in -te, which means yourself: buckle yourself in. Kids all over Mexico and the Southwest ask ¿Ya llegamos? on every road trip!

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Are we there yet?"
How do you say "I'm thirsty"?

lessons.title: Left, right and straight
lessons.goal: Give and follow directions: left, right, straight, at the light and at the corner.

dialogue.es: Abuela, ¿a la derecha o a la izquierda?
Sí. En el semáforo, da vuelta a la izquierda.
dialogue.en: Yes. At the traffic light, turn left.

dialogue.es: No, Sofía. En la esquina, a la derecha.
dialogue.en: No, Sofía. At the corner, to the right.

tip.title: Derecha or derecho?
tip.text: A la derecha means to the right. Derecho means straight ahead, as in Sigue derecho. Only the last letter is different, so listen closely. In Mexico you'll hear both da vuelta and dobla for turn.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Go straight"?

exercises.es: ¿A la derecha o a la izquierda?

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Not yet"?

lessons.title: Where's the gas station?
lessons.goal: Ask where a place is, say if it's near or far, and ask the driver to stop.

dialogue.en: Dad, the gas station! On the right.
Thanks, Dad! Are we going home?

tip.title: Está for places
tip.text: Use está to say where something is or how near it is: Está cerca, it's close; Está lejos, it's far. ¿Dónde está...? asks where something is. In Para aquí, para means stop (from parar), not for.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "It's far"?
How do you say "to the right"?

lessons.title: How much is it?
lessons.goal: Ask what something costs and say if it's cheap or expensive.

dialogue.en: Mom, I want to buy this.
A book? How much does it cost?
It's cheap. Do you have money?

dialogue.es: Mamá, quiero comprar esto. Cuesta cien dólares.
dialogue.en: Mom, I want to buy this. It costs a hundred dollars.
Now we're going to the supermarket.

tip.title: Cuesta or cuestan?
tip.text: Cuesta is for one thing; cuestan is for more than one: ¿Cuánto cuestan los zapatos? In the US the price is in dólares, and in Mexico it's in pesos: cinco dólares, cinco pesos. Esto means this, for something you're pointing at.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "How much does it cost?"
How do you say "It's close"?

lessons.title: At the checkout
lessons.goal: Pay by card or in cash, get your change and receipt, and answer about a bag.

dialogue.en: Good afternoon. How much is it?

dialogue.es: En efectivo. Aquí tiene, cuarenta dólares.
dialogue.en: Cash. Here you go, forty dollars.

dialogue.es: Gracias. Aquí tiene el cambio y el recibo. ¿Necesita una bolsa?
dialogue.en: Thank you. Here's your change and the receipt. Do you need a bag?
Here you go. See you later!

tip.title: Usted at the store
tip.text: Store clerks and customers usually speak to each other with usted, the polite you. That's why the clerk asks ¿Necesita una bolsa?, not ¿necesitas? Aquí tiene means here you go, and both people say it when they hand over money, change or a bag.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Do you take cards?"
How do you say "It's very expensive"?

lessons.title: Shopping for clothes
lessons.goal: Say you're just looking, ask for another color and say something is too big.

dialogue.es: Hoy no, Mateo. Necesitas una camisa.
dialogue.en: Not today, Mateo. You need a shirt.

dialogue.es: Señora, ¿tiene otro color? No quiero gris.
dialogue.en: Ma'am, do you have another color? I don't want gray.

dialogue.es: Sí, aquí tiene una camisa verde.

dialogue.en: Mom, it's too big on me.

tip.title: Me queda
tip.text: Me queda grande means it fits me big, so it's too big. For something too small, say me queda chico, or me queda chica for a girl word like la camisa. La ropa (clothes) is one word for many things, so it takes la and es: la ropa es nueva. In Mexico you'll also hear nada más estoy viendo for I'm just looking.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I'm just looking"?
How do you say "in cash"?

lessons.title: What's the weather like?
lessons.goal: Ask about the weather and say it's hot, cold, cool, sunny, windy or nice.

dialogue.es: Hace sol y hace buen tiempo.
dialogue.en: It's sunny and the weather is nice.

dialogue.es: No, no hace viento. Ponte la gorra, por favor.
dialogue.en: No, it isn't windy. Put on your cap, please.

dialogue.es: Sí. Y aquí en la noche hace fresco.
dialogue.en: Yes. And here at night it's cool.

dialogue.es: Sí, en la tarde hace calor. Aquí está el agua.
dialogue.en: Yes, in the afternoon it's hot. Here's the water.

tip.title: Hace calor or tengo calor?
tip.text: Spanish uses hace (it makes) for most weather: hace calor, hace frío, hace sol. Hace calor is about the weather, and tengo calor is about how you feel. Buen loses its o before a word like tiempo: hace buen tiempo. In an Arizona summer you'll say both hace calor and tengo calor!

exercises.prompt: How do you say "What's the weather like?"
How do you say "the shirt"?

lessons.title: A monsoon storm
lessons.goal: Say it's cloudy, clear or raining, that rain is coming, and name the sky's sights.

dialogue.en: Mom, is it going to rain today?
I don't know. Right now it's clear.
Mom, a big cloud! It's cloudy.

dialogue.es: No te preocupes, Mateo. Estoy aquí.

dialogue.en: Mom, the sun and the rain!

tip.title: Está for right now
tip.text: For weather happening right now, Spanish uses está: está lloviendo, it's raining; está nublado, it's cloudy. Va a llover means it's going to rain. In Arizona, a summer storm often ends with sun and rain at the same time, and that's when you look for an arcoíris.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "It's raining"?
How do you say "Put on your cap"?

lessons.title: The four seasons
lessons.goal: Name the seasons and say what the weather is like in each one.

dialogue.es: En el invierno, el diez de diciembre.
En el invierno hace fresco aquí.
dialogue.en: In the winter it's cool here.

dialogue.es: Sí. Y en el verano, ¡qué calor!
dialogue.en: Yes. And in the summer, it's so hot!

dialogue.es: Mi cumpleaños es en la primavera, en abril.
dialogue.en: My birthday is in the spring, in April.

dialogue.es: En la primavera hace buen tiempo.
dialogue.en: In the spring the weather is nice.

dialogue.es: En el otoño hace sol y hace fresco.
dialogue.en: In the fall it's sunny and cool.

tip.title: Seasons with el and la
tip.text: Seasons take el or la: la primavera, el verano, el otoño, el invierno. To say in the summer, use en: en el verano. Like days and months, seasons are written without a capital letter in Spanish.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "summer"?

exercises.en: Say: In the summer it's hot.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "It's going to rain"?

lessons.title: Head and face
lessons.goal: Name the parts of the head and face, and tell someone to brush their teeth.

dialogue.es: Sí. Lávate los dientes, por favor.
Muy bien. Ahora, ¿dónde está la nariz?
dialogue.en: Very good. Now, where's your nose?

dialogue.es: ¡Aquí está la nariz! Y la boca.
dialogue.en: Here's my nose! And my mouth.

dialogue.es: Aquí, los ojos. Y las orejas.
dialogue.en: Here, my eyes. And my ears.
Good night, Mateo. I love you.

tip.title: The teeth, not your teeth
tip.text: Body words come with el, la, los or las. Spanish says Lávate los dientes, wash the teeth, because it's clear whose teeth they are. In Mexico, lavarse los dientes is the everyday way to say brush your teeth.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "the nose"?
How do you say "It's bedtime"?

lessons.title: What hurts?
lessons.goal: Name parts of the body and say what hurts.

dialogue.en: Sofía, are you okay? Where does it hurt?

dialogue.es: Me duele la pierna. Y el pie.
dialogue.en: My leg hurts. And my foot.

dialogue.es: Y yo... me duele la cabeza.

tip.title: Me duele, me duelen
tip.text: Spanish says it hurts me: Me duele la cabeza, my head hurts. If more than one thing hurts, use duelen: Me duelen los pies. La mano is a girl word even though it ends in o.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "My head hurts"?
How do you say "the eyes"?

lessons.title: At the doctor
lessons.goal: Say you're sick, describe a fever or a cough, and wish someone well.

dialogue.en: I'm sick, Mom. I have a cough.

dialogue.es: Hola, mi hijo está enfermo. Necesito un doctor, por favor.
dialogue.en: Hello, my son is sick. I need a doctor, please.
Hi, Mateo. Where does it hurt?

dialogue.es: Me duele la cabeza. Y tengo fiebre. ¡Achú!
dialogue.en: My head hurts. And I have a fever. Achoo!

dialogue.es: Mucha agua y a dormir, Mateo.
dialogue.en: Lots of water, and off to bed, Mateo.

tip.title: ¡Salud!
tip.text: When someone sneezes, say ¡Salud!, which means health. Que te mejores means get well soon; to a grown-up you don't know well, say que se mejore. A girl or woman who is sick says Estoy enferma.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I have a fever"?
How do you say "My feet hurt"?

lessons.title: Pets
lessons.goal: Name pets and say what pet you have.

dialogue.en: Hi, Sofía. Do you have a dog?

dialogue.es: No. Tengo un gato. Se llama Nube.
dialogue.en: No. I have a cat. His name is Nube.

dialogue.es: Yo tengo un perro, un pájaro y un pez.
dialogue.en: I have a dog, a bird and a fish.

dialogue.es: Se llama Chato. El perro es grande.
dialogue.en: His name is Chato. The dog is big.
And my uncle has a horse!

tip.title: Un and una
tip.text: Un and una mean a: un perro, un gato, una lagartija. Tengo un gato means I have a cat. Careful: el pez is a live fish, and fish you eat is el pescado. Nube (cloud) is a fun name for a gray and white cat.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "the bird"?
How does a boy say "I'm sick"?

lessons.title: Desert animals
lessons.goal: Name the animals of the Sonoran Desert and point one out.

dialogue.es: Sí, el coyote está lejos. No te preocupes.
dialogue.en: Yes, the coyote is far away. Don't worry.
And a roadrunner in the street!

dialogue.es: No está aquí, Mateo. No te preocupes.
dialogue.en: It isn't here, Mateo. Don't worry.

tip.title: ¡Mira!
tip.text: ¡Mira! means look! and it's how you point something out: ¡Mira, un coyote! Correcaminos is made of corre (runs) and caminos (roads), so it really is a road runner. In Sonora and Arizona, people call the javelina el jabalí, and more than one are jabalíes.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "the roadrunner"?
How do you say "The dog is big"?

lessons.title: A walk in the desert
lessons.goal: Talk about cactus, mountains and the monsoon, and warn someone about thorns.

dialogue.en: Yes. And here, a prickly pear cactus.
Mateo, watch out for the thorns!

dialogue.es: Sí. Es el monzón. Va a llover.
dialogue.en: Yes. It's the monsoon. It's going to rain.

tip.title: The monsoon
tip.text: In Arizona, the summer storm season is called el monzón; in Mexico many people say la temporada de lluvias, the rainy season. Sahuarita's name is said to come from sahuarito, a little saguaro. Bonito changes to bonita for a girl word: la montaña es muy bonita.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "the prickly pear cactus"?

exercises.en: Say: Watch out for the thorns.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "the lizard"?

lessons.title: A table for four
lessons.goal: Ask for a table and the menu, ask what's good, and order a drink.
new: Una mesa para cuatro, por favor.
Un vaso de agua, por favor.

dialogue.es: Buenas noches. Una mesa para cuatro, por favor.
dialogue.en: Good evening. A table for four, please.
Sofía, what do you want to drink?

dialogue.es: Un vaso de agua, por favor.

tip.title: Tomar means drink
tip.text: At the table, tomar usually means to drink: ¿Qué quieres tomar? Customers and servers speak with usted, so you ask the server ¿Qué me recomienda? A waiter is el mesero and a waitress is la mesera.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "A table for four, please"?
exercises.answer: Una mesa para cuatro, por favor.
wrong: Una mesa para dos, por favor.
What do you want to drink?

exercises.en: What do you want to drink?

pairs: Un vaso de agua, por favor.
What do you want to drink?

exercises.en: Say: A table for four, please.
exercises.es: Una mesa para cuatro, por favor.

exercises.answer: Un vaso de agua, por favor.
wrong: Una mesa para cuatro, por favor.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "the desert"?

lessons.title: Ordering food
lessons.goal: Order politely, ask for something with or without, and ask if it's spicy.

dialogue.es: Y frijoles. Con queso, por favor.
No pica mucho. La salsa roja sí pica.
dialogue.en: It's not very spicy. The red salsa is spicy.
Mom, it IS spicy! Water, please!

tip.title: Quisiera and pica
tip.text: Quisiera means I'd like; it's softer and more polite than quiero. In Mexico, pica means it's spicy: ¿Pica? asks is it spicy?, and No pica mucho means it's not very spicy. Salsa verde and salsa roja can both be spicy, so it's always good to ask!

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I'd like some tacos"?
How do you say "What do you recommend?"

exercises.es: Un vaso de agua, por favor.

lessons.title: Dessert and the check
lessons.goal: Say the food is delicious and you're full, order to go, and ask for the check.

dialogue.en: I want dessert! And french fries.
French fries? Mateo! The check, please.

dialogue.es: Y el postre, ¿para aquí o para llevar?
dialogue.en: And the dessert, for here or to go?

tip.title: Asking for the check
tip.text: In many restaurants in Mexico, the server won't bring the check until you ask for it: La cuenta, por favor. That's being polite, not slow. A boy or man says Estoy lleno, and a girl or woman says Estoy llena.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "The check, please"?

wrong: Una mesa para cuatro, por favor.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "the money"?

lessons.title: Ser and estar
lessons.goal: Use ser for who or what someone is and estar for where they are and how they feel.
new: Mi mamá está en el trabajo.

dialogue.es: Sí, es mi casa. Me llamo Sofía. Soy estudiante.
dialogue.en: Yes, it's my house. My name is Sofía. I'm a student.

dialogue.es: Mucho gusto, Sofía. Soy de Sonora. ¿Y tú?
dialogue.en: Nice to meet you, Sofía. I'm from Sonora. And you?

dialogue.es: Somos de Arizona. Mi mamá está en el trabajo.
dialogue.en: We're from Arizona. My mom is at work.
I'm at home, Dad. And you?

dialogue.es: Estoy en el carro con Mateo. Él está cansado.
dialogue.en: I'm in the car with Mateo. He's tired.

dialogue.es: Papá, hay una señora nueva aquí. Ella es muy simpática.
dialogue.en: Dad, there's a new lady here. She's very nice.

dialogue.es: ¡Papá, ya llegamos! Estamos en la tienda.
dialogue.en: Dad, we're here! We're at the store.

tip.title: Ser or estar?
tip.text: Spanish has two verbs for to be. Ser is for what someone or something is: Soy estudiante, Somos de Arizona, Ella es muy simpática. Estar is for where something is and how it is right now: Estoy en el carro, Él está cansado. Spanish often leaves out I and we, because the verb ending already says who.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "We're from Arizona"?

exercises.es: Mi mamá está en el trabajo.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "The check, please"?

lessons.title: Have and go
lessons.goal: Say what you have, what you have to do, and where you're going.

dialogue.en: Hi, Mateo. Where are you going?

dialogue.es: Voy a la escuela. Mi papá va al trabajo.
dialogue.en: I'm going to school. My dad is going to work.

dialogue.es: ¡Tengo un perro! Se llama Pecas. ¿Tienes tiempo?
dialogue.en: I have a dog! His name is Pecas. Do you have time?
No, I have to go. It's late!

dialogue.es: En la tarde tenemos tarea, Sofía y yo.
dialogue.en: In the afternoon we have homework, Sofía and I.

dialogue.es: ¿Y el sábado? Vamos al parque con Pecas.
dialogue.en: And on Saturday? Let's go to the park with Pecas.
Yes! Let's go to the park on Saturday.

tip.title: Al means a + el
tip.text: Ir (to go) changes with who is going: voy (I go), vas (you go), va (he or she goes), vamos (we go). A and el join into al: al parque, al trabajo, but a la escuela stays apart. Tengo que plus a verb means I have to: Tengo que irme, I have to go.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Where are you going?"
How do you say "I'm in the car"?

lessons.title: Want, can and need
lessons.goal: Say what you want and don't want, offer help, and ask for help.

dialogue.es: Sofía, quiero jugar. ¿Quieres venir al parque?
dialogue.en: Sofía, I want to play. Do you want to come to the park?
I don't want to. I have homework.

dialogue.es: Mateo, ¿puedes ayudarme? Necesito ayuda en la cocina.
dialogue.en: Mateo, can you help me? I need help in the kitchen.

dialogue.es: Papá, ¿puedes ayudarme? No entiendo la tarea.
dialogue.en: Dad, can you help me? I don't understand the homework.
And later we go to the park?

tip.title: Quiero and puedo plus a verb
tip.text: After quiero (I want) and puedo (I can), the next verb stays in its dictionary form: quiero jugar, puedo ayudar. To ask someone, change the ending: ¿quieres? ¿puedes? The me on the end of ayudarme means me: help me.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Can you help me?"

exercises.en: Say: Do you want to come?

exercises.prompt: How do you say "We're at the store"?

lessons.title: What, where and when
lessons.goal: Ask what something is, what someone is doing, where things are and when things happen.

dialogue.en: Hi, Mateo. What are you doing?
Hi, Emilio. What do you want to do?

dialogue.es: Vivo cerca, en la calle Nopal.
dialogue.en: I live close by, on Nopal Street.
Mom, when are we going to the park?
And Sofía's party? When does it start?

tip.title: Accents on question words
tip.text: Question words always carry an accent mark: qué, dónde, cuándo. Without the accent, que and cuando are ordinary words in a sentence, like that and when. Use dónde for where something is, and adónde for where someone is going.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Where's the bathroom?"

wrong: What do you want to do?

exercises.en: What do you want to do?
Say: What do you want to do?

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Can you help me?"

lessons.title: Who and why
lessons.goal: Ask who and why, answer with because, and check if something is okay.

dialogue.es: Es mi prima, Ana. Es muy simpática.
dialogue.en: She's my cousin, Ana. She's very nice.
Mom, Mateo doesn't want ice cream.

dialogue.es: Mateo, un poco de helado y a dormir. ¿Está bien?
dialogue.en: Mateo, a little ice cream and then bed. Is that okay?
The ice cream is tasty, right?

tip.title: Por qué or porque?
tip.text: Why is por qué: two words, with an accent. Because is porque: one word, no accent. Porque sí is the classic kid answer, just because! Put ¿verdad? at the end of a sentence to make it ask right?: Está rico, ¿verdad?

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Why?"

lessons.title: How many and which one
lessons.goal: Ask how much and how many, which one, and if you can join in.

dialogue.en: How much water do you want, Isabel?
There are apples and bananas. Which one do you want?
Isabel, how many brothers and sisters do you have?

dialogue.es: Mi color favorito es el verde. ¿Cuál es tu favorito?
dialogue.en: My favorite color is green. Which one is your favorite?

tip.title: Cuánto changes
tip.text: Cuánto matches the word after it: cuánto tiempo, cuánta agua, cuántos hermanos, cuántas horas. Agua is a girl word even though we say el agua, so it's cuánta agua. Cuál means which one, when you choose from a few things.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "How many brothers and sisters do you have?"

wrong: What do you want to do?

exercises.en: How much water do you want?

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Just because"?

lessons.title: I like it!
lessons.goal: Say what you like and don't like, and agree with me too and me neither.

dialogue.en: Yes, I like it a lot.

dialogue.es: A mí también. ¿Te gustan los tacos?
dialogue.en: Me too. Do you like tacos?

dialogue.es: ¡Sí! Sin cebolla. No me gusta la cebolla.
dialogue.en: Yes! Without onion. I don't like onions.

dialogue.es: Me gusta el chocolate. ¿Y a ti?
¡A mí también! Y me gustan los perros.
dialogue.en: Me too! And I like dogs.

tip.title: Me gusta works backward
tip.text: Me gusta el chocolate literally says chocolate pleases me. Use gusta for one thing and gustan for more than one: me gustan los perros. To agree, say A mí también (me too); to agree with a no, say A mí tampoco (me neither). ¿Y a ti? asks and you?

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I like dogs"?

exercises.en: Say: Yes, I like it a lot.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Where do you live?"

lessons.title: Things we love to do
lessons.goal: Say what you, your family and your friends like to do.
new: A mi hermana le gusta bailar.

dialogue.en: Mateo, what do you like to do?

dialogue.es: Me gusta jugar videojuegos. ¡Y me encanta nadar!
dialogue.en: I like playing video games. And I love swimming!

dialogue.es: A mi hermana le gusta bailar. Y le gusta dibujar.
dialogue.en: My sister likes to dance. And she likes to draw.

dialogue.es: Y me gusta leer. ¡Me encantan los libros!
dialogue.en: And I like to read. I love books!

dialogue.es: Los domingos nos gusta ir al parque.
dialogue.en: On Sundays we like going to the park.

dialogue.es: ¡Qué bueno! Vamos al parque el domingo.
dialogue.en: That's great! Let's go to the park on Sunday.

tip.title: Me, te, le, nos
tip.text: Me gusta is I like, te gusta you like, le gusta he or she likes, and nos gusta we like. For things to do, use the verb's dictionary form: me gusta leer, me encanta nadar. Me encanta is stronger than me gusta, like love compared with like. In A mi hermana, mi has no accent because it means my; mí with an accent means me.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I love swimming"?

exercises.en: We like going to the park.

pairs: We like going to the park.

exercises.en: Say: What do you like to do?

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Me neither"?

wrong: What do you want to drink?

lessons.title: Favorites
lessons.goal: Say which one you like better, what you prefer, and what you don't like at all.

dialogue.es: Sofía, para la mochila, ¿cuál te gusta más, el azul o el rojo?
dialogue.en: Sofía, for the backpack, which one do you like better, blue or red?

dialogue.es: Me gusta más el azul, mamá.

dialogue.en: Mom, what is there to eat?

dialogue.es: Hay tacos o pizza. ¿Cuál te gusta más?
dialogue.en: There's tacos or pizza. Which one do you like better?
Oh, no! I don't like it at all.

tip.title: Más means better here
tip.text: To say you like something better, add más: Me gusta más el azul. ¿Cuál te gusta más? asks which one do you like better? Prefiero (I prefer) does the same job. No me gusta nada is a strong no: I don't like it at all.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I prefer pizza"?

exercises.answer: I don't like it at all.

exercises.en: Which one do you like better?

pairs: I don't like it at all.
Which one do you like better?

exercises.es: ¿Cuál te gusta más, el rojo o el azul?

exercises.prompt: How do you say "She likes to draw"?

lessons.title: What are you going to do?
lessons.goal: Say what you're going to do today with voy a and ask about someone's plans.
new: Primero la tarea, luego a jugar.

dialogue.en: Sofía, what are you going to do today?
I'm going to do my homework.

dialogue.es: Mateo, primero la tarea, luego a jugar.
Ay, mamá. Tengo hambre. Voy a comer.
dialogue.en: Oh, Mom. I'm hungry. I'm going to eat.

dialogue.es: Está bien. Y luego, la tarea.
Mateo, vamos al parque. ¿Vas a venir?
dialogue.en: Mateo, we're going to the park. Are you going to come?
I'm tired. I'm going to sleep.

tip.title: Ir a plus a verb
tip.text: To talk about what's going to happen, use voy a, vas a, va a, vamos a or van a, then the verb as it is in the dictionary: voy a comer. Vamos a jugar can mean let's play or we're going to play. Primero ... luego means first ... then.

tip.title: A before people
tip.text: When you visit or call a person, Spanish puts a in front of them: visitar a los abuelos, llamar a mi abuela. English doesn't say this a at all. For things there's none: ver una película. Los abuelos can mean the grandparents, Grandma and Grandpa together.

tip.title: Esta noche and después
tip.text: Esta noche means tonight (this night), and esta mañana means this morning. Después means afterward. Salir means to leave or go out, so ¿A qué hora vamos a salir? asks what time we're leaving. Cenar means to have dinner, from la cena.

Me fue muy bien. Aprendí algo nuevo.

Great! And you, Mateo? What did you do today?

tip.title: Past forms with accents
tip.text: Many past forms for I end in an accented é or í: terminé, jugué, aprendí, perdí. Stress the end, because the accent changes the meaning: termino is I finish, terminé is I finished. Jugué gets a u so the g stays hard. Se me olvidó is how most people say I forgot; it's like saying it slipped my mind.

tip.title: Fui and fuimos
tip.text: Fui means I went and fuimos means we went; they come from ir. Fui can also mean I was, and the rest of the sentence makes it clear. Ganamos can mean we won or we win; words like ayer or el sábado tell you which.

It's late! Let's go to school.
I'm sorry, teacher. We arrived late.

tip.title: Anoche and ayer
tip.text: Anoche means last night, and ayer means yesterday. Llovió is the past of llover, to rain: it rained. ¿Qué pasó? asks what happened, and people also use it to ask what's wrong. Like ganamos, llegamos can mean we arrived or we arrive.

tip.title: Up, down, on and off
tip.text: Subir means to go up or turn up, and bajar means to go down or turn down: subir el volumen, bajar el volumen. Prender means turn on and apagar means turn off: prende la luz, apaga la luz. In the car, el aire means the air conditioning.

lessons.goal: Ask if someone's hungry, suggest a stop, and enjoy the view out the window.

tip.title: Mucha hambre
tip.text: Hambre is a girl word even though we say el hambre, so it's mucha hambre, not mucho. Spanish often uses the present for the near future: Llegamos en diez minutos means we'll be there in ten minutes. ¿Paramos a comer? is a friendly way to suggest a stop.

tip.title: The little word ya
tip.text: Ya means already or now, and it changes the feel of a sentence: ¿Ya llegamos? asks are we there yet?, Ya casi llegamos says we're almost there, and ¡Ya llegamos! says we're here. Cuéntame means tell me, a warm way to start a conversation. Y yo a ti is a sweet answer to Te quiero: and I (love) you.
